topics: 🗡️ The Roman Quaestor's Ram — an old bechor's ear is slit, the Sages permit it once, then draw the line
👦 Children and the Lambs' Tails — the mishna's rule: intentional blemish forbids, accidental permits
🐏 Kicking a Pursuing Firstborn — does timing prove intent to blemish?
🤰 Blemishing Before Birth — Rav Yehuda's leniency for a firstborn still in the womb
👥 Whose Testimony Is Trusted? — Israelite shepherds, priest shepherds, and the incentive to lie

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Intent, Incentive, and Credibility
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 35a–35b
overview.hebrewSource: זֶה הַכְּלָל: כֹּל שֶׁהוּא לְדַעְתּוֹ — אָסוּר, שֶׁלֹּא לְדַעְתּוֹ — מוּתָּר
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Two mishnayot open the daf with real-world stories: a Roman official slits the ear of an aging, unslaughtered firstborn ram, and children playing in a field accidentally sever a lamb's tail. In both cases the Sages permit that first, unintended blemish — but once people start deliberately imitating it, they forbid the practice for anyone who acts 'with knowledge.' A further mishna asks about kicking an animal that is chasing you, and a side discussion allows causing a blemish on a firstborn fetus before birth. The daf closes with a major new mishna: since priests benefit financially from a firstborn's blemish, are priest-shepherds trusted to testify that a blemish occurred naturally, the way Israelite shepherds are?

slides.title: 🗡️ The Quaestor's Ram and the Children's Lambs
slides.subtitle: Two mishnaic stories teach the same rule from different angles

steps.content: 1️⃣ A Roman quaestor asks why an old, shaggy ram (a firstborn) hasn't been slaughtered; told it needs a blemish, he slits its ear himself
2️⃣ The Sages permit that ram's slaughter — but once the quaestor starts slitting other firstborns' ears on purpose, they forbid those
3️⃣ Separately, children tying lambs' tails together accidentally sever one tail (a firstborn's); the Sages permit it — but forbid it once people start tying tails deliberately

4️⃣ Both stories are needed: the gentile case alone might not extend to a Jewish minor (who could form a habit), and the minor's case alone might not extend to a gentile adult (who could be confused with a Jewish adult)

callout.label: The rule:
callout.text: "Whatever is done with intent (לְדַעְתּוֹ) is forbidden; whatever is done without intent is permitted" — including even indirect causation, but excluding a gentile who blemished after hearing an offhand remark, not a direct question.

slides.title: 🗣️ 'It Had a Blemish' vs. 'A Blemish Was Made'
slides.subtitle: Does the bystanders' phrasing to the quaestor change the halakha?

lines.speaker: Rav Ḥisda
lines.text: The ram was permitted only because they told him 'unless it has a blemish' — implying a natural one. Had they said 'unless a blemish is made on it,' that is like telling him outright: go and blemish it!

lines.speaker: Rava
lines.text: Not so — both phrasings are passive and refer to something that happens on its own. There is no difference between them; either way the animal remains permitted.

callout.label: Why it matters:
callout.text: The exact words used to describe a blemish can be read as an invitation to cause one — or as a neutral description of a natural event.

slides.title: 🐏 New Mishna: Kicking a Pursuing Firstborn
slides.subtitle: If a firstborn animal chases its owner and he kicks it, causing a blemish, may he slaughter it?
rows: Presumed to be self-defense, not intent to blemish
Rav Pappa: presumed intent to render it slaughterable, not mere anger
Rav Pappa (alt.): presumed to be delayed anger recalling the earlier distress, not intent to blemish

callout.label: Underlying test:
callout.text: Every case in this sugya turns on the same question: was the blemish caused with intent to render the animal slaughterable, or incidentally?

slides.title: 🤰 Blemishing Before Birth
slides.hebrewSource: מוּתָּר לְהַטִּיל מוּם בִּבְכוֹר קוֹדֶם שֶׁיָּצָא לַאֲוִיר הָעוֹלָם
slides.label: Rav Yehuda's ruling:
slides.text: It is permitted to cause a blemish in a firstborn fetus before it emerges into the air of the world, since its sanctity begins only at birth. Rava applies this practically: a kid's long ears emerge first from the birth canal, so its ear can be blemished in utero; a lamb's short ears do not, so its lip is the practical target instead (some say a lamb's ears can work too, if it emerges through its temples).

slides.title: 👥 New Mishna: Whose Word Can Be Trusted?
slides.subtitle: Shepherds may testify a blemish was natural — but priests have a motive to lie

boxes.title: Israelite Shepherds
items: Trusted to testify the blemish was not caused intentionally
No personal financial stake in the outcome

boxes.title: Priest Shepherds
items: Not trusted — they may profit if the firstborn becomes blemished and is given to them
Two amora'im (R' Yoḥanan/R' Elazar) dispute whether this means priests employed by an Israelite, or Israelites employed by a priest

boxes.title: Two Refinements
items: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: a priest IS trusted about another priest's firstborn, just not his own
Rabbi Meir: anyone suspect on this matter may not judge or testify at all, even for someone else

callout.label: Halakha:
callout.text: The Gemara ultimately rules like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel — a priest's own son or daughter may testify for him, but not his wife, 'since a wife is like himself.'

summary.principle: A blemish caused with intent to permit slaughter disqualifies the firstborn from ever being slaughtered on its account, and whoever stands to gain financially from a blemish — chiefly a priest regarding his own firstborn — is not a credible witness that it occurred naturally.

flowSteps.content: 🗡️ Quaestor's ram, children's lamb tail: first accidental blemish permitted; deliberate copycats forbidden
🐏 Kicking a pursuing firstborn: timing and presumed intent determine the outcome
🤰 A firstborn fetus may be blemished before birth, since sanctity begins only then

columns.content: 👥 Israelite shepherds trusted — no stake in the outcome
👥 Priest shepherds not trusted — stand to gain from the blemish

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: intent and incentive together decide both whether a blemish counts and whose testimony about it is believed

quiz.q: In the mishna's story, why did the Sages permit the ram's slaughter after the Roman quaestor slit its ear, but then forbid it once he began slitting other firstborns' ears?
o: Because the first blemish was unintentional, while the later ones were done with the deliberate intent to make the animals slaughterable
Because the ram was old and the others were young
Because Roman officials were never trusted at all
Because the first ear-slitting was invalid as a blemish
quiz.e: The general principle stated in the mishna is that a blemish caused with intent (לְדַעְתּוֹ) forbids slaughter, while one caused without intent permits it — the quaestor's first act was incidental, his later ones deliberate.

quiz.q: According to Rav Pappa's first version, what is the halakha if a person kicks his pursuing firstborn animal only after the pursuit has already ended?
o: It is always permitted, since he acted out of self-defense
It is forbidden, since he is presumed to have intended to cause a blemish rather than merely react to distress
It is permitted only on Shabbat
It depends solely on the animal's age
quiz.e: In the first version, kicking after the pursuit ends is presumed to be a deliberate attempt to blemish the animal, not a reflexive act of self-defense, so the animal remains forbidden.

quiz.q: Why does Rav Yehuda permit causing a blemish on a firstborn animal while it is still a fetus?
o: Because fetuses feel no pain
Because the animal's sacred status as a firstborn only takes effect once it is born, 'emerges into the air of the world'
Because it is never really a firstborn until weaned
Because fetal blemishes are automatically excluded from the halakha
quiz.e: Since sanctity as a firstborn begins only at birth, causing a blemish before that point does not violate the prohibition against blemishing consecrated animals.

quiz.q: According to the mishna, why are priest-shepherds generally not trusted to testify that a blemish on a firstborn occurred naturally?
o: Priests are never trusted about any halakhic matter
They may stand to financially benefit if the animal becomes blemished and is given to them to eat
Priests cannot serve as witnesses under any circumstances
Their testimony requires two additional witnesses regardless
quiz.e: The mishna's concern is a conflict of interest: since a priest may benefit from a firstborn's blemish, his testimony that it occurred naturally is not automatically trusted the way an Israelite shepherd's is.

quiz.q: What distinction does Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel draw regarding a priest's credibility to testify about a blemished firstborn?
o: A priest is never trusted under any circumstances
A priest is trusted regarding another priest's firstborn, but not regarding his own
A priest is trusted only regarding his own firstborn
There is no difference between an Israelite's and a priest's testimony
quiz.e: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that a priest lacks a personal financial motive to lie about someone else's firstborn, but does have one regarding his own — and the Gemara rules like him.
